sections.section_title: Case Presentation and Initial Obstetric Assessment
sections.description: Introduces the patient’s demographics, presenting symptoms in mid-gestation, bedside evaluation, and early supportive measures, framing the clinical problem that prompted further investigation.
subtopics: Patient profile: obese nulliparous woman in her 40s at 21 weeks’ gestation with normal aneuploidy screening and fetal morphology
Presenting symptoms: acute left upper quadrant and pelvic pain with mild dyspnoea
Vital signs and cardiopulmonary assessment: normal oxygen saturation, heart rate, blood pressure, and ECG
Abdominal and pelvic examination: distended abdomen with an 18 cm taut-elastic mass; bimanual exam revealing a fixed, hard 9 cm pelvic mass bulging the posterior fornix
Initial symptom control: paracetamol and semi-orthostatic positioning reducing pain and dyspnoea
Intercurrent findings: low-grade fever, urinary Klebsiella pneumoniae infection; iron-deficiency anaemia and pregnancy-consistent leukocytosis/CRP rise
Problem representation: mid-trimester pregnancy with two large abdominal-pelvic masses, pain, restrictive symptoms, and uncertain origin

sections.section_title: Pregnancy-Safe Diagnostic Workup: Imaging and Laboratory Interpretation
sections.description: Details the stepwise use of ultrasound, color Doppler, and non-contrast MRI in pregnancy, and contextualizes tumor markers to refine risk and guide management.
subtopics: Ultrasound findings: two unilocular cystic masses with regular margins and peripheral vascularization; upper mass 18×12×7 cm in left subphrenic region; lower mass 9.5×8×8 cm adherent to a 58×71 mm posterior intramural–subserosal myoma with cystic degeneration
Tumor markers in pregnancy: CA 19-9, CA 15-3, CEA, β2-microglobulin, LDH normal; CA-125 mildly elevated (41.8 U/mL) with upward trend—limitations and normative trimester context

Non-contrast MRI after first trimester: thick-walled cysts with inhomogeneous T1/T2 fat-sat fluid; focal T1–T2 hyperintense solid areas; no adenopathy; unclear cleavage plane for caudal mass suggesting continuity with uterus
Imaging safety principles: ultrasound as first-line; non-contrast MRI at ≤1.5 T acceptable after first trimester; avoid gadolinium unless exceptional indications
Why CT and gadolinium were avoided: fetal radiation exposure and gadolinium-associated risks
Dyspnoea mechanism supported by imaging: mass effect causing restrictive physiology rather than cardiopulmonary disease
Limitations of preoperative imaging: gravid uterus and mass ‘steric bulk’ obscuring stalks/feeding vessels

sections.description: Explains how imaging and clinical features differentiate decidualised endometriomas from cystic/degenerating leiomyomas, and reviews the pregnancy-specific biology of fibroids relevant to this case.
subtopics: Decidualised endometrioma vs cystic/degenerating leiomyoma: typical ultrasound/MRI clues (shading on T1, papillary projections with decidualisation, continuity with myometrium, vascular patterns)
Pedunculated subserosal leiomyoma: propensity for torsion, ischemia, leakage, and fever; correlation with acute pain
Cystic degeneration in leiomyomas: pathophysiology, imaging appearance, and implications for mass consistency and size
CA-125 interpretation: physiologic trimester peaks, benign elevations (endometriosis, myoma), and low specificity for malignancy in pregnancy
Leiomyoma size dynamics in pregnancy and puerperium: early gestational growth, later stabilization, and postpartum regression
Symptom generation: mass effect causing diaphragmatic elevation and restrictive dyspnoea; pelvic outlet obstruction risk from low posterior myoma
Oncologic risk estimation: absence of ascites/adenopathy, unilocular morphology, pregnancy context lowering suspicion yet not excluding malignancy

sections.section_title: Maternal–Fetal Management Strategy: Indications, Operative Choices, and Peripartum Planning
sections.description: Outlines the decision-making that led to surgery in the second trimester, intraoperative tactics prioritizing pregnancy preservation, and longitudinal obstetric planning including delivery mode.
subtopics: Indications for surgery in pregnancy: escalating pain/dyspnoea, risk of torsion/rupture/infection, diagnostic uncertainty, and anticipated uterine/mass growth
Timing: rationale for second-trimester intervention (21+6 weeks) as the safest operative window when necessary
Approach selection: reasons for midline longitudinal laparotomy over laparoscopy (mass size, multiplicity, intramural/posterior location, gestational age)

Intraoperative steps: peritoneal fluid for culture/cytology; fetal cardiac activity checks pre/during/post; identification of a large, vascular, twisted, leaking pedunculated cystic leiomyoma; double-clamp excision and hemostatic closure of stalk
Conservative choice for the caudal mass: leaving the fixed intramural–subserosal leiomyoma in situ to minimize obstetric risk
Uterotonic/tocolytic strategy: progesterone prophylaxis perioperatively and during follow-up; evidence considerations and goals (reduce uterine irritability)
Infectious management: antibiotic prophylaxis (cefazolin) and targeted therapy for Klebsiella UTI (cephalosporin plus clarithromycin per antibiogram) compatible with pregnancy
Hematologic support: management of iron-deficiency anaemia with IV iron and red cell transfusions postoperatively
Postoperative surveillance: maternal recovery, serial obstetric assessments every 3 weeks for fetal growth and amniotic fluid
Delivery planning: elective caesarean at 37 weeks due to obstructive posterior isthmic myoma; reuse of midline incision; considerations to reduce labour dystocia and uterine scar stress

sections.description: Summarizes maternal–neonatal outcomes and pathology, and distills clinical principles and a practical approach for managing large atypical abdominal masses during pregnancy.
subtopics: Pathology and cytology: benign leiomyomas with ischemic necrosis near twisted pedicle; peritoneal fluid negative
Maternal–neonatal outcomes: symptom relief, anaemia correction, uncomplicated recovery, healthy term neonate
Residual disease course: pelvic myoma size reduction to 7.5 cm postpartum, patient asymptomatic and opting for expectant management while breastfeeding

Key lessons: prioritize ultrasound then non-contrast MRI; interpret CA-125 cautiously; reserve surgery for complications or oncologic concern; tailor intervention to preserve pregnancy and avoid overtreatment
Intraoperative fetal safety: document fetal heart rate pre/intra/post procedure
Delivery mode determination: base on mass size, number, location (obstruction risk) rather than diagnosis alone
Team-based care: importance of multidisciplinary planning (obstetrics, gynecology, surgery, anesthesia, radiology, neonatology) and individualized risk–benefit analysis

Practical algorithm: symptomatic mass → US+Doppler → if indeterminate, MRI (no gadolinium) → risk assessment (malignancy vs complication) → conservative care if stable; operate in second trimester for torsion/rupture/infection, intractable symptoms, or significant diagnostic uncertainty; plan delivery based on residual anatomy
